extracted.intended_audience: British military officers, colonial administrators, and military tacticians (readers of campaign memoirs/policy-makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and judgments about employing cavalry on the Indian frontier, civil–military responsibilities in field forces, medical/logistical practice in campaign operations, and related policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cavalry reconnaissance as a legitimate duty
rubrics_metrics.description: "this legitimate duty of cavalry—reconnaissance." Cavalry should be employed more and more for reconnaissance; they can easily move over broken country and, when boldly used, can collect as much information as is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major Beatson made daily expeditions to valleys and passes; though horsemen need good ground to fight on to advantage, they can still perform reconnaissance in difficult terrain. The use of cavalry for reconnaissance on the frontier — previously thought dangerous — is advocated as effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cavalry role in protecting flanks in mountain actions
rubrics_metrics.description: In mountain actions cavalry are usually tasked to protect a flank where the ground rarely admits of charging in formation; men must use carbines and operate in small dismounted groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical method: form little groups of six or seven dismounted men firing carbines; keep mounted patrols concealed in nullahs/hollows/behind obstacles to gallop out and chase attackers who advance from bad ground. This holds enemy groups in check and prevents them from participating in the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cavalry tactics to cover foraging parties and retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of patrol lines and dismounted troops to present difficult targets and provide covering fire so mounted troops can mount and withdraw under protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a squadron covered a foraging party by line patrols; dismounted men fired from cover while other troops remained concealed; mounting was staged (first troop mounts while second covers), troops spread into extended line and cantered to cover while the remaining troops kept up rapid fire to cover retirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cavalry for offensive charges and pursuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Cavalry are formidable in offensive tactics — charges and vigorous pursuit inflict heavy losses and can turn the tide of an engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples (Shabkadr, Swat Valley, Landakai) show charges and pursuits by 11th Bengal Lancers and Guides Cavalry produced decisive results. Cavalry frequently were 'the first in, and the last out' and were praised in official despatches for tactical skill and gallantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy: deploy British cavalry across the frontier alongside native regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of refusal to allow British cavalry across the frontier; recommendation that British and native troops be employed in a regular proportion: when two native cavalry regiments have been sent on service across the frontier, the third so sent shall be British.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: excluding British cavalry is a 'penny wise' policy that discourages professional soldiering, reduces officer ambition and regimental keenness, and is poor economy given training and motivational benefits of active service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow subalterns to volunteer for attachment to native cavalry
rubrics_metrics.description: To give cavalry subalterns opportunities of seeing active service, they should be allowed to volunteer for emergency employment with native cavalry and be attached after passing Hindustani and approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed mechanism: subalterns, with colonel's approval, attached to native regiments after qualifying in Hindustani and being reported fit; counters argument of financial difficulty by noting officers' eagerness and possible economies. Intended to supply native regiments short of officers and to give British subalterns experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active service as essential soldier training
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent small engagements and being under fire are of the greatest value in training soldiers; exposure reduces imagined danger and increases effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: a soldier's first under-fire experience makes him fear every shot, but repeated exposure yields understanding of odds and greater effectiveness — the 'firing produced very little effect' on experienced troops; implies deliberate provision of active experience for training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical evacuation and convoy protection to preserve force mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve force mobility, send all sick and wounded to base at once; convoys must be properly escorted because a long straggling string of doolies and animals in broken ground is vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical details: slight cases on camels (kajawas), serious cases in doolies/litters borne by four natives, convalescents ride mules; infantry escort disposed along the line with every precaution; journey is painful but necessary to maintain operational mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary/disease prevention is an operational necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns produce long and serious sick lists from diseases like typhoid caused by drinking surface water and exposure; generals must watch hospital returns as carefully as enemy movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: control of water quality, camp sanitation, and measures to prevent fevers are essential to maintain fighting strength; moving men from unhealthy stations increases vulnerability to summer fevers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility for wounded soldiers and veterans
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a wretched and discreditable system that the state neglects soldiers who have served it, leaving their care to charity and newspaper philanthropy; the burden should be proudly borne by the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of inadequate pensions and post-service support; suggests that officers/regiments may supplement pensions but argues this is government responsibility and a moral duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of duties: civil officers vs military command in Field Forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties of civil officers in a campaign are twofold: (1) to negotiate, and (2) to collect information. Civil officers are indispensable for negotiation but should not usurp military authority; diplomatic duties to civil officers, conduct of war to military officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: intelligence collection should primarily be by Pathan Sepoys, the Intelligence Branch and enterprising cavalry who understand military needs; civil officers must be under the control of the General directing operations — 'There must be no "Imperium in imperio."' Assign responsibility clearly to avoid vacillation and disasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local khans and jirgahs in securing surrender and negotiating terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Local rulers (e.g., Khan of Khar) and jirgahs can be instrumental in persuading tribes to surrender rifles, make submissions, and pledge peace terms; full durbars formalize ratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Khan of Khar urged peace and secured initial rifle surrenders; durbar with tribesmen and khans led to formal submission and swearing to terms; use local intermediaries for negotiation and to secure compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about the feasibility and cost of total disarmament
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'total disarmament of the frontier tribes' is desirable, obtaining it would be as painful and tedious as 'to extract the stings of a swarm of hornets, with naked fingers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: weigh the human and financial cost of forcible disarmament against its desirability; small tangible gains (a few rifles) may have cost large lives and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautionary entrenchment of camps despite assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when local protectors promise safety, camps should be entrenched as a matter of form rather than reliance on assurances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: although the Khan of Jar offered pickets to watch the camp, the troops entrenched themselves 'not... because we doubted our protector's powers... but merely as a matter of form.' Practical rule: adopt defensive measures regardless of diplomatic assurances.
